content: Addressing inequalities and promoting equal opportunities in education and the workforce can foster gender equality, social inclusion, and cohesion. Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) within a lifelong learning framework can create diverse learning pathways with multiple entry and exit points, supporting both educational and career progression. These pathways enable learners to move between different levels or locations and acquire recognized skills and qualifications throughout their lives. Together, such networks and pathways can form more adaptable and responsive lifelong learning systems. (UNESCO 2015c) Maternity Leave (or Pregnancy Leave): This refers to employment-protected leave for working women around the time of childbirth or, in some countries, adoption. The International Labour Organization (ILO) convention on maternity leave mandates a minimum leave period of 14 weeks. (OECD 2017e) Generalist Medical Doctor or Physician: Generalist medical practitioners (ISCO 2008 code 2211), including family and primary care doctors, diagnose, treat, and prevent illnesses, injuries, and physical or mental impairments. They maintain general health in humans by applying modern medical principles and procedures. These professionals plan, supervise, and evaluate care and treatment plans implemented by other healthcare providers. They do not restrict their practice to specific diseases or treatment methods and may provide ongoing, comprehensive medical care to individuals, families, and communities. (International Labour Organization 2012) Specialist Medical Doctor: Specialist medical doctors (ISCO 2008 code 2212) diagnose, treat, and prevent illnesses, injuries, and impairments using specialized diagnostic, medical, surgical, physical, and psychiatric techniques. They apply modern medical principles and procedures, plan and supervise care, and evaluate treatment plans carried out by other healthcare providers. Specialists focus on specific disease categories, patient types, or treatment methods and may engage in medical education and research within their chosen fields. Examples include gynecologists (specialists in women's reproductive health), obstetricians (specialists in pregnancy and childbirth), and pediatricians (specialists in children's development, care, and diseases). (International Labour Organization 2012) Midwife: Midwifery professionals (ISCO-2008 code 221) plan, manage, provide, and evaluate care services before, during, and after pregnancy and childbirth. (International Labour Organization 2012) Net Inflow and Outflow of Health Workers: Net inflow refers to the difference between the number of health workers entering the labor market and those leaving it in a given year, where more workers enter than leave. Conversely, net outflow occurs when more workers leave than enter. (WHO 2015c) Newly Active Health Worker: A health worker who begins practicing in a specific profession during a given year. (WHO 2015c) Nurse Practitioner: A registered or advanced practice nurse with expert knowledge, complex decision-making skills, and clinical competencies for expanded practice. These characteristics are shaped by the context or country in which they are credentialed to practice. A master’s degree is recommended for entry-level practice. (ICN 2017) Nurse Professional: As defined by ISCO-2008 code 2221, nursing professionals treat and care for individuals who are physically or mentally ill, elderly, injured, or disabled. (International Labour Organization 2012) Occupation: An occupation is defined as a set of jobs with similar tasks and duties. A job refers to tasks and duties performed by one person, either for an employer or through self-employment. National Health Workforce Accounts should ideally cover health and health-related occupations grouped according to the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08). (International Labour Organization 2012, International Conference of Labour Statisticians 2013) Occupational Health and Safety: This field involves anticipating, recognizing, evaluating, and controlling workplace hazards that could harm workers' health and well-being, considering potential impacts on surrounding communities and the environment. (Alli 2008) Official Development Assistance (ODA): ODA refers to official financial flows aimed at promoting economic development and welfare in developing countries. These flows are concessional, with a grant element of at least 25%, and include contributions from donor government agencies to developing countries and multilateral institutions. Export credit agency lending for export promotion is excluded. (OECD 2015b) Parental Leave: Employment-protected leave for working parents, often supplementary to maternity and paternity leave, and frequently following maternity leave in some countries. (OECD 2017e) Part-Time Employment: Individuals in employment (either as employees or self-employed) who typically work less than 30 hours per week in their main job. (OECD 2017g) Paternity Leave: Employment-protected leave for working fathers around the time of childbirth or shortly thereafter. (OECD 2017e) People-Centered Care: This approach to care prioritizes the perspectives of individuals, families, and communities as active participants in and beneficiaries of trusted health systems. It emphasizes humane and holistic responses to their needs and preferences, ensuring they are educated and supported to make decisions and participate in their care. This care model is organized around people’s health needs rather than diseases. (WHO Regional Office for Europe 2017) Primary Care Team: A group of professionals with complementary roles in patient care, reflecting a broader societal trend toward mutual respect, shared responsibility, and cooperation, rather than deference and hierarchy. (WHO Regional Office for Europe 2017) Primary Object of Attack: This includes individuals, infrastructure, vehicles, and other health-related items subjected to violence, obstruction, or threats. Examples include healthcare facilities (e.g., hospitals, clinics), healthcare providers (e.g., physicians, nurses, midwives), healthcare transport (e.g., ambulances), and healthcare recipients (e.g., patients, visitors). (WHO 2017a) Public Expenditure: Spending from public funds, which include state, regional, and local government bodies and social security schemes. Public capital formation includes publicly financed investments in facilities and capital transfers to the private sector for construction and equipment. (OECD 2011c) Public Health Workforce: A diverse group of professionals responsible for core public health activities, such as disease surveillance, population health assessment, identification of priority health problems, and preparedness for public health emergencies. These activities also include health protection operations and evaluation of prevention efforts. (Bjégovic-Mikanovic et al. 2014) Qualified Educator: Educators with the minimum academic qualifications required to teach a subject at the relevant level in a given country. (UNESCO 2017) Registered Health Worker: Health workers whose data are included in a health workforce registry, regardless of their activity status or license validity. (WHO 2015c) Rural-Urban Classification: This classification defines urban and rural areas based on population size, density, or access to key services. Urban areas are often defined first, with rural areas identified by exclusion. Administrative units may contain both urban and rural populations. (OECD et al. 2011) Self-Sufficiency in the Health Workforce: Strategic investment in national infrastructure to achieve an optimal, stable, and appropriately distributed health workforce through effective recruitment and retention policies and programs. (Pan American Health Organization 2011) Sex: The biological determination of an individual’s sex at birth. (WHO 2015c) Skill Mix: This term refers to the combination or grouping of different staff categories in the workforce, the roles and activities they perform, or the mix of posts, grades, or occupations within an organization. It can also describe the mix of skills available at a specific time or within a facility. (Buchan and O’May 2000, Buchan and Calman 2004) Social Accountability: The obligation of an authorized body to direct its education, research, and service activities toward addressing the priority health concerns of the community, region, or nation it serves. (Boelen and Heck 1995) Social Determinants of Health: The conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age, as well as the broader forces and systems shaping these conditions, including economic policies, social norms, and political systems. (WHO 2008b) Specialist Surgical Workforce: This includes licensed, qualified physician surgeons, anesthesiologists, and obstetricians. (International Labour Organization 2016) Student: An individual not economically active who attends a regular educational institution for systematic instruction at any level. (OECD 2017f) Subnational Level: Defined based on a country’s specific conditions, governing structures, and constitutional provisions. Disaggregation by administrative boundaries down to the first or second subnational level is recommended, with examples including states, regions, provinces, counties, and districts. (OECD et al. 2011) Transformative Health Workforce Education: The sustainable expansion and reform of health workforce education and training to increase the quantity, quality, and relevance of health workers, thereby strengthening national health systems and improving population health outcomes. (World Health Assembly 2013, UNESCO 2015c) Tuition Fee: The money students pay to health workforce education and training institutions for their instruction. Unemployment: Individuals of working age who are qualified for a job, not employed, actively seeking employment, and available to take up a job opportunity. (Eurostat 2017a) Vacancy Rate: The proportion of total posts that are vacant, expressed as a percentage of all positions, both filled and unfilled.
